summary: A status report on the network numbers and autonomous system numbers in use in the Internet community. It was replaced by RFC 1166.

eli5.summary: Every network has a number, like a street number. This is a list of who had which numbers at the time.

subtitle: A 1989 status report listing the assigned IP network numbers and autonomous system numbers.

tldr.problem: Operators needed one place to see which network numbers and autonomous system numbers had been handed out, and to whom.
tldr.mechanism: The SRI-NIC published a periodically updated registry: the class A, B and C network numbers with names and contacts, the EGP autonomous system numbers, and totals of how many were assigned.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot that was replaced by RFC 1166, which is itself the later report in the series. It records the address classes of the time rather than defining a protocol.

today: RFC 1117 is an Informational snapshot that has been obsoleted by RFC 1166, so its tables are historical and not a current record of assignments.

sections.title: A Registry in an RFC
sections.content:
RFC 1117 is, in its own words, an official status report on the network numbers and the autonomous system numbers used in the Internet community. It documents the currently assigned numbers and says the RFC will be updated periodically. Current information could be had from Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI International.

Each listed network or autonomous system names a responsible person, shown as a bracketed code such as [nn,iii]. The letters are a NIC Handle, a unique identifier in the NIC WHOIS/NICNAME service. The document follows the usual RFC conventions of decimal numbers and big-endian bit diagrams.

The header lists a long chain of older number RFCs that this one obsoletes, including RFC 1062 and RFC 1020.
sections.eli5: This is the official list kept by one office. If you wanted to know who owned a number, you looked it up here or asked the office.

sections.title: The Address Classes
sections.content:
IP uses a 32-bit address split into a network part and a local part. This RFC describes four forms, or classes, told apart by the highest-order bits.

  • Class A: first bit 0, a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address. This allows 128 class A networks.
  • Class B: first bits 1-0, a 14-bit network number and a 16-bit local address. This allows 16,384 class B networks.
  • Class C: first bits 1-1-0, a 21-bit network number and an 8-bit local address. This allows 2,097,152 class C networks.
  • Class D: first bits 1-1-1-0, used for multicast.

No addresses are allowed with the four highest bits set to 1-1-1-1. These are called class E and are reserved.
sections.eli5: An address has two parts, like a street name and a house number. Depending on the kind of network, more of the address is the street and less is the house, or the other way round.

sections.title: Notation, Categories and Special Addresses
sections.content:
Addresses are written in dotted decimal: four 8-bit fields as decimal numbers separated by periods. The RFC's example is VENERA.ISI.EDU at 10.1.0.52. In the listings, rrr stands for the local address part.

Each listed network carries a one-letter code for its category of user: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-defense) and C for Commercial. An asterisk marks independent networks that use the IP protocols but have to apply separately to interconnect with the Internet. A T marks an old number kept during a transition, with the network name suffixed -TEMP.

A few addresses have fixed meanings. Address zero means "this", so 0.0.0.37 could mean host 37 on this network. All ones means "all", so 128.9.255.255 could mean all hosts on network 128.9. Class A network 127 is the loopback network: a datagram sent to it should loop back inside the host and never appear on any network.
sections.eli5: Some numbers are reserved for special jobs. One of them means "talk to myself", so a computer can send a message that never leaves the machine.

sections.title: Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content:
The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) lets groups of gateways form autonomous systems, and it provides a 16-bit field to identify them. This part of the RFC registers the values of that field.

The table gives a number, a system name and a contact. It starts with 1 for The BBN Core Gateways, 2 for DCN-AS and 3 for The MIT Gateways, and continues through many university, laboratory and company systems. The RFC cites the EGP specifications as RFC 827 and RFC 888.
sections.eli5: Big groups of routers get their own ID number so that other groups know whose network is whose.

sections.title: Totals and How Space Was Divided
sections.content:
The report closes the network section with counts. For the ARPA-Internet and DDN-Internet it shows 33 class A, 767 class B and 2,666 class C networks assigned, 3,466 in total. For "Internet and independent uses" it shows 33, 1,524 and 12,613, for 14,170 in total.

Appendix A explains that the number space in each class is divided among Research, Defense, Government and Commercial uses. Class A, for example, allocates 8 to Research and 24 each to Defense and Government. Because networks can move between categories, for example when an experimental network becomes operational, the spaces are assigned individually rather than by a simple partition, and the count per use must stay within the stated limits.

Organizations not yet connected to the Internet may be given numbers for non-connected service. If they connect later, with the proper approvals, they do not need to be renumbered.
sections.eli5: The list also counts how many numbers are used and how many are left, and says the numbers are shared out between research, military, government and business.
